# Numerical torsion lift from closed divisors

2026-11-12. Scoped classical bridge, independently source-checked in
`audits/reviews/2026-11-12-surface-mascot-lift.md`. This advances the native
surface comparator by paying numerical lifting once a faithful arithmetic
model is available. It does not pay reconstruction precision or that model.

## Exact statement

Given a genus-g curve with good reduction at P, an actual point O, a faithful
separable plane/function-field presentation of its good special curve, and
polynomial-size exact generic Riemann--Roch coordinates, an actual prime-to-P
ell-torsion class represented by closed divisors can be lifted to precision
P^E with polynomial bit cost in the presented sizes, g, numerical E, residue
extension degree, log P and log ell. No geometric support splitting is needed.
This is classical Mascot/Khuri-Makdisi arithmetic; no quantum advantage follows.

For d0=2g+1 and D0=d0 O, a class D-gO becomes D'=D+(d0-g)O,
represented by L(2D0-D'). Closed-place RR constructs this subspace. One common
residue field of polynomial degree supplies more than 5d0 evaluation points
away from denominators and exceptional loci: Hasse--Weil and factoring random
projection fibres give a polynomial capped clock. Unit derivatives lift them
over one unramified local extension. Their supports are independent of D.

Compute exact RR functions in a common-denominator normal form and saturate
their coefficient lattice. Faithful reduction and a nonzero reduced denominator
give independent reduced rational functions. Integrality of evaluations at
more than deg(D0) points forces genuine section integrality: a primitive
nonintegral section scaled into H0(D0) would otherwise have too many zeros
on the special curve. Nakayama then certifies the full integral RR lattice.
Use all products/constraints and full linear systems in the source's practical
randomized shortcuts; these variants remain polynomial.

At each precision-doubling step Mascot Algorithm10 lifts any Jacobian point
modulo P^e to P^(2e), then multiplies by N=0 mod P^e, N=1 mod ell. The error
lies in J_e/J_(2e), whose formal-group law is additive because the ideal is
square-zero; its exponent divides P^e. This proves unique torsion lifting,
including P=2, without the source's excessive global logarithm claim.

## Decisive corrections and remaining inputs

* Good reduction of the abstract curve alone is insufficient. Replacing y
  by Y=P y changes a good equation into Y²=P²f(x), with nonreduced displayed
  reduction. The faithful presentation and RR coordinate-size bound are
  explicit upstream obligations, not supplied by the words "good reduction".
* The source's blanket log:J1->P O^g isomorphism fails at two. On
  y²+xy=x³+4x+1, discriminant -4225, T=(-1/4,1/8) is nonzero 2-torsion
  reducing to O with formal parameter 2. The square-zero proof repairs the
  algorithm, not that assertion.
* Unique effective degree-g extraction requires residue h0(T+gO)=1.
  Its Abel differential then has zero kernel and cokernel by RR, so the
  divisor lifts with unit pivots, even with nonsplit or nonreduced support.
  Generic-characteristic-zero h0=1 alone is insufficient.
* Original Frobenius requires conjugation of O and the appropriate divisor
  correction. A row permutation needs the source's stable evaluation/base
  data. Numerical lift uniqueness does commute with arithmetic Frobenius.

The primary source is Mascot, arXiv:1808.03939, retained July2019 text,
Algorithms9/10, Theorem2.23 and Remark1.6:
`audits/sources/surface_module_2026/mascot_lift.{pdf,txt}`. Remark1.6 explicitly
leaves rational reconstruction uncertified without a height bound. The paid
`2026-11-12-closure-lift` call ended empty/truncated and supplies no evidence;
the independent source proof above is separately recorded.

Next decisive obligation: construct a faithful good auxiliary-prime model
and polynomial-size exact RR coordinates from the growing-degree native
cover, and bound canonical torsion coordinates. No full classical point count,
uniform reconstruction precision, speedup, hardness or separation is claimed.

# Surface torsion lifting: Mascot source and model prerequisites

2026-11-12. Independent source/algorithm audit. Read current `STATE.md`,
`SURFACE_NATIVE_TORSION_MODULE.md`, and the actual primary
`audits/sources/surface_module_2026/mascot_lift.txt`: Sections 2, 4, 5,
especially Remark 2.4, Theorem 2.23, Algorithms 9 and 10, and Remark 1.6.
Source PDF SHA256:
`4da85f621b32b68e2673c71bc8b8cac7bfe1666fbd4c9f975c181a2474811880`.
No Git, network, API, archive search, code, or numerical control.
Interpreter, if needed: `/opt/anaconda3/bin/python`.

## Result and exact input boundary

Mascot's Algorithm 10 pays prime-to-`P` torsion lifting to a prescribed
NUMERICAL precision once a compatible integral evaluation model is
available. Its finite-field input may be an actual torsion class represented
by CLOSED divisors: its geometric support need not split, and those support
points need not be the auxiliary evaluation points. One polynomial-degree
common unramified field suffices for the evaluation model.

The integral model can be constructed by the RR/coefficient-lattice method
below if the supplied plane chart reduces faithfully to the GOOD special
curve and the exact RR functions have a charged polynomial-size coordinate
presentation. This explicitly removes an additional requirement to supply
integral RR bases or independently reduced evaluation matrices.

Do not replace that presentation condition by the mere assertion that an
abstract curve has good reduction. A generic separable plane equation need
not reduce faithfully. For example, replacing `y` by `Y=P y` changes a good
hyperelliptic equation into `Y^2=P^2 f(x)`, whose displayed reduction is
nonreduced. Mascot does not construct a compatible smooth model from an
arbitrary such presentation. The upstream native-cover construction must
provide/check a good presentation (or explicitly repair it), including
the relevant coordinate and RR-size bounds. No new arithmetic height bound
for that upstream construction is proved here.

Under this model condition, the lift has polynomial bit cost in genus,
presented model/RR/divisor size, residue extension degree, numerical output
precision, `log P`, and `log ell`. The construction is independent of full
ambient torsion splitting and independent of geometric divisor-support
splitting. It does NOT certify rational reconstruction or a global height.

## 1. Closed divisors supply the actual finite-field Jacobian input

Let `C` have genus `g>=1`, good reduction at the unramified prime `P`,
and a supplied actual rational point `O` with good reduction. Put

```
d0=2g+1,       D0=d0 O,       V_j=L(jD0).
```

Suppose the supplied actual torsion class is represented over the residue
field by `T=D-gO`, with `D` a rational effective CLOSED divisor of degree
`g`. Set `D'=D+(d0-g)O`. Then `D'` is effective of degree `d0`,
`[D'-D0]=T`, and

```
W_D=L(2D0-D')=L((d0+g)O-D)
```

has the required dimension `d0+1-g`. Finite-field RR on closed-place
ideals computes this subspace and its evaluations without splitting the
support of `D`. If the input is another degree-zero divisor presentation,
ordinary RR first gives an equivalent effective presentation of degree
`d0`; no prime-support representative theorem is needed.

Verify the supplied relation `[ell]T=0` in the finite Jacobian, using its
exact divisor/RR representation. Neither the source nor this review
substitutes an arbitrary matrix for an actual torsion class. Source
Remark 1.7 expressly warns that most matrices of the right dimensions
do not represent Jacobian points.

## 2. Constructing one evaluation field and the auxiliary points

Let the common residue field already containing the input data be
`k0=F_(P^a)`. Work with a separable affine plane chart of the good special
curve. Let `d` be the projection degree and let `T_bad` bound the number
of geometric points excluded by:

* poles and exceptional places of the chosen chart;
* vanishing of the selected unit derivative for point lifting;
* `O` and the denominators of the chosen RR function presentation.

This is a numerical degree bound computed from the presented functions
and is polynomial in their charged sizes. Choose a SINGLE extension
`k=F_(P^(a s))` large enough that

```
#C(k) >= |k|+1-2g sqrt(|k|) > T_bad+5d0+1.
```

A field size larger than `(4g+2T_bad+2(5d0+1)+2)^2` is more than
sufficient. Thus `s=O(1+log(g+T_bad)/log |k0|)` suffices. This is a
degree bound, not enumeration of that field, and all auxiliary points
are constructed over this same field.

A bounded randomized construction samples the plane coordinate `x`,
factors the degree-at-most-`d` fiber polynomial, and retains rational
points passing the exclusions. With a slightly generous version of the
above size bound there are at least `|k|/2` admissible rational points.
Their images occupy at least `|k|/(2d)` coordinate values. Consequently
each trial succeeds with probability at least `1/(2d)`, up to excluding
the already selected `O(g)` points. This gives a polynomial capped clock
for `n_Z=5d0+1` distinct evaluation points, with a stated FAIL probability.
Finite-field factorization and arithmetic are charged in the field's
explicit degree and `log P`. No common field for unrelated divisor
support degrees is formed.

Lift these evaluation points to the unramified integer ring `O_K` by
fixing a lift of the free coordinate and using the unit partial
derivative to Hensel-lift the other coordinate. This is quadratic
lifting with no loss of digits. The residue points remain distinct,
and the lifted points are actual curve points in ONE unramified local
field of degree `a s`.

For torsion lifting alone, `Z` need not be stable under the original
`P`-Frobenius. If Mascot's row-permutation Frobenius Algorithm 8 is also
used, its stated conditions must hold: `D0` and `Z` must be defined over
the arithmetic base, and the permutation must be recorded. Taking
unions of Frobenius orbits in the chosen single field supplies a stable
`Z` at polynomial cost (possibly slightly increasing `n_Z`). If `O`
is not defined over that original base, its conjugation/basepoint change
must be included, just as in the native-module note. No uncorrected
row-permutation formula is asserted in that case.

## 3. The integral RR bases are constructible under the good-presentation check

This is the specific bridge not supplied merely by quoting Mascot.
Assume the exact generic RR calculation gives a basis of `L(D0)` in
polynomial-size rational-function coordinates in the supplied separable
plane function field. Choose one common denominator and reduce the
numerators to a normal form of degree below the plane polynomial's
degree in `y`. Require that the reduced plane function field is the
actual good special curve, with the same normal-form degree, and that
the common denominator is nonzero after primitive reduction.

Take the coefficient vectors of these normal-form numerators and compute
their saturated lattice over the local integer ring. Exact coefficient
linear algebra gives a basis whose coefficient columns are independent
modulo `P`. With an exact number-field/function-field presentation this
is a finite lattice computation; its valuations and bit costs are
bounded by the sizes of the supplied RR coefficient matrices. If only
unconditioned finite approximations to those matrices are supplied, this
argument is NOT a license to infer exact rank from them.

The resulting functions have integral values at the chosen evaluation
points because their common denominator is a unit there. They form
the true integral `H0(D0)` lattice, for the following reason. On the
smooth proper good model, `H0(O(D0))` is a free lattice of rank
`d0+1-g`, and its reduction is the full special-fiber RR space: degree
`d0>2g-2` makes `H1` vanish. For any generic section, take the least
power `P^k` making it integral. If `k>0` while all its evaluation values
are integral, the nonzero reduction of that primitive integral section
vanishes at more than `d0` distinct points away from `O`. This is
impossible for a nonzero section of degree `d0`. Hence evaluation
integrality already implies membership in the true lattice.

Finally, independent reduced normal-form coefficient columns give
independent rational functions on the faithful special curve. Thus the
constructed integral sections have `d0+1-g` independent reductions and
are an integral RR basis by Nakayama. No numerical formal-log inversion,
support splitting, or torsion-coordinate height enters this argument.

Evaluation at `n_Z>5d0` points is injective on `V5`, over both the
generic and special curves. Starting from this `V1` basis, the source's
multiplication constructions therefore build `V2`, `V3`, their equation
matrices, and the other required spaces with unit pivots and independent
reductions. Normal generation at degree at least `2g+1` supplies the
required product-space dimensions.

This gives a constructive RR/saturation route, not a theorem that ANY
generic plane presentation automatically has a faithful reduction or
polynomial generic RR coordinate sizes. Those checks belong to the
presented-curve input and upstream arithmetic model construction. The
source itself says at the beginning of Section 2 that constructing an
explicit `V1` basis can depend on the model and assumes it available.

## 4. No unbounded generic-choice retries are needed for the lift

The source describes practical randomized shortcuts, but a polynomial
clock need not rely on its “rare failure” comments:

* In DivAdd, compute ALL pairwise products of basis sections and take
  their span; the degree hypothesis proves surjectivity.
* In DivSub, impose the constraints from ALL basis sections. The source
  explicitly gives this option when dimension is not known in advance.
* In Algorithm 9, solve the full polynomial-size linear system instead
  of selecting random combinations of its equations.

These choices increase the genus exponent but remain polynomial. The
known RR dimensions and good reductions give the rank hypotheses of
Theorem 2.23 where it is used. Arbitrary p-adic matrices with unknown
characteristic-zero rank are not being admitted. The actual Jacobian
point and the high-degree effective-divisor presentation are essential
to this regularity argument.

Algorithm 9 then lifts a valid point modulo `P^e` to a valid point
modulo `P^(2e)`. Its geometric existence and the source's membership/
tangent-space construction are separate from merely lifting its matrix
entries. Properness/smoothness of the good model supplies actual points
behind these finite-level representatives.

## 5. Algorithm 10, uniqueness, and the characteristic-two correction

Assume `ell!=P`. The finite etale group scheme `J[ell]` gives a unique
`ell`-torsion lift of every residue `ell`-torsion point over the same
unramified local field. In a precision-doubling stage, any lifted point
differs from that torsion lift by an element of `J_e/J_(2e)`. This
quotient has exponent `P^e`. Hence an integer

```
N=0 mod P^e,          N=1 mod ell
```

removes the difference while preserving the desired torsion point.
This is exactly Algorithm 10. `N` can be chosen below `ell P^e`, so its
addition-chain length is `O(log ell+e log P)`. There are `O(log E)`
stages to output precision `P^E`. Ring arithmetic in the unramified
degree-`a s` extension has polynomial bit cost in `a s`, `E`, and
`log P`; together with Algorithm 9 this proves the stated lifting bound.

The source justifies the finite-layer exponent by claiming
`log:J1 -> P O_K^g` is an isomorphism. That assertion is false as
written at `P=2`, even with good reduction and an unramified base.
A concrete symbolic example is

```
E: y^2+xy=x^3+4x+1,       discriminant=-4225.
T=(-1/4,1/8).
```

The discriminant is odd, `T` satisfies the equation, and
`-(x,y)=(x,-y-x)` fixes `T`, so it is nonzero rational 2-torsion.
It reduces to the origin and has formal parameter `-x/y=2`.
Any formal logarithm kills this torsion, so it cannot be injective on
all of `J1`.

Algorithm 10 nevertheless remains valid at two: for EVERY smooth
commutative formal group, the ideal `P^e/P^(2e)` is square-zero, so
the formal group law there is its additive tangent law. This directly
identifies `J_e/J_(2e)` with the corresponding additive Lie module
and proves the exponent, without any global logarithm assertion.
Alternatively the available auxiliary restriction `P>2g` avoids two
for `g>=1`. Neither route changes the prime-to-`P` torsion hypothesis.

If the original torsion class was defined over the smaller residue
field before the evaluation-field enlargement, uniqueness implies its
lift descends to the corresponding smaller unramified field. Temporary
evaluation coordinates do not enlarge the intrinsic torsion field.
The same uniqueness makes lifting compatible with arithmetic Frobenius.

## 6. Canonical degree-g divisors are a separate regularity condition

Suppose one also wants the unique effective divisor in the class
`T+gO`. The necessary loss-free condition is

```
h0(C_bar, T_bar+g O_bar)=1
```

on the RESIDUE curve, not just `h0=1` on the characteristic-zero generic
fiber. At an effective divisor `D` of degree `g`, the tangent kernel of
the Abel map `Sym^g C -> Pic^g C` is
`H0(O(D))/H0(O)`. Its cokernel is `H1(O(D))`. Riemann--Roch makes
both vanish when `h0(D)=1`. Thus the Abel map is etale there, and
the residue divisor has a unique compatible Hensel lift along the
lifted line bundle. RR with independent reduction computes the
one-dimensional section space, or the corresponding closed-divisor
ideal, with unit-pivot precision.

The divisor can be retained as a closed effective Cartier divisor;
its individual geometric support need not split and may be nonreduced.
The required condition and the corresponding divisor/ideal chart must
be certified. If the residue class lies on the special locus where
`h0>1`, Mascot's arbitrary effective degree-`d0` representation still
lifts the torsion POINT, but this canonical degree-`g` extraction is
not supplied by the same unit-Jacobian argument.

## Unchanged global boundary

The source's Remark 1.6 explicitly says its subsequent identification
of p-adic values with rational coefficients is not guaranteed correct
and requires certification. None of the lifting arguments above bounds
the heights needed for that identification. A polynomial numerical
precision lifting algorithm is not a polynomial native reconstruction
precision theorem.

Accepted: closed-divisor conversion, one common polynomial-degree
evaluation field, actual evaluation-point lifts, the integral RR
saturation bridge under the stated faithful-presentation check, and
prime-to-`P` torsion lifting with a finite precision clock. Corrected:
the source's global logarithm assertion at two. Separate: residue
`h0=1` canonical-divisor extraction. Open upstream: the native
arithmetic good-model/RR presentation and uniform coordinate/height
bounds whenever they are not already supplied by the charged model.
No full surface point-counting or rational-reconstruction theorem is
claimed by this scoped lift result.

21: Resolving singularities is a central problem in computational algebraic geometry.
22: In this paper we describe a new algorithm for resolving singularities of irreducible
23: plane curves. The algorithm runs in polynomial time in the bit complexity model,
24: does not require polynomial factorization, and works over Q or any finite field.

35: taining the Puiseux coefficients, leading to an algorithm that is polynomial in
36: the number of base field operations. However, the algorithm is not analyzed

70: Let R be an algebraic function field over an algebraically closed field K, i.e., a

75: parameter.

77: x − a, denoted x = a, plus one place with local parameter 1/x, denoted x = ∞.

79: some unit u ∈ P and positive integer c. The number c is called the ramification
80: index of P over p. Every place p of K(x) extends to at least one place P of R.
81:     Now let f (x, y) = 0 be an irreducible plane curve of degree n in y with
82: coefficients in K, and let R = K(x)[y]/f . A place p of K(x) is called simple if
83: for any two places P, P0 of R over p, P ∩ K(y) 6= P0 ∩ K(y), and all places of

89: 2.1   Statement of the Problem
90: 
91: The problem we consider in this paper is as follows. Given an irreducible plane
92: curve f (x, y) = 0 with coefficients in some subfield k ⊆ K, determine all the
93: exceptional places p of K(x). For each such p, determine the set of places P
94: of R over p. For each such P, determine its ramification index over p, a local

99: in terms of x and y.
100:     In the solution of this problem, all computation should take place in the
101: subfield k. In practice, k will usually be Q or a finite field.
102: Example 1. Consider the hyperbola y 2 = x2 − 1. There are three exceptional

142: 2.2   Efficient Birational Reparametrization
143: A critical subroutine is birational reparametrization, or change of variables. We
144: will often wish to reparametrize an irreducible plane curve f (x, y) = 0 in terms of
145: new parameters u, v that are rational functions of x, y. We will need to compute
146: the defining equation g(u, v) = 0 of the curve in terms of the new parameters.
147:      The problem of birational reparametrization of algebraic surfaces has an
148: efficient solution in general, using multivariate gcds. For our application, all
149: cases we will encounter will be of the following special form:
150:                            u = (x − a)s (y − b)−t + c                           (1)
151:                                         −n           m
152:                             v = (x − a)         (y − b) + d
153: 
154: 
155:                                            3
156: where a, b, c, d ∈ K and s, t, m, n ∈ Z such that sm − tn = ±1. Any such map is
157: invertible, and its inverse is of the same form:
158: 
159:                              x = (u − c)m (v − d)t + a
160:                               y = (u − c)n (v − d)s + b
161: 
162: We can reparametrize efficiently as follows:
163:  1. Substitute (u − c)m (v − d)t + a for x and (u − c)n (v − d)s + b for y in f to
164:     obtain f ((u − c)m (v − d)t + a, (u − c)n (v − d)s + b).
165:  2. Multiply or divide by appropriate powers of u − c and v − d as necessary to
166:     clear denominators and eliminate extraneous factors of the form u − c and
167:     v − d.
168: The resulting polynomial g(u, v) is the irreducible representation of the plane
169: curve f (x, y) = 0 in terms of the parameters u, v.
170: Example 2. Consider the irreducible curve y 2 = x3 − x4 and the map u = x2 /y,
171: v = y 2 /x3 . This is a birational map of the form (1) with (s, t, m, n) = (2, 1, 2, 3)
172: and a = b = c = d = 0. Its inverse is x = u2 v, y = u3 v 2 . To reparametrize in
173: terms of u, v, substitute u2 v and u3 v 2 for x and y, respectively, in the equation
174: of the curve to get u6 v 4 = u6 v 3 − u8 v 4 and eliminate the factor u6 v 3 , leaving
175: the irreducible equation v = 1 − u2 v. Rewriting this as v = 1/(1 + u2 ), we see
176: that the curve is of genus zero and that u is a generator of the function field.

178: 2.3   Squarefree Decomposition
179: Another key subroutine is squarefree decomposition. One wishes to transform
180: a set A of polynomials into another set A0 such that the elements of A0 are
181: squarefree and pairwise relatively prime, and every element of A is a product of
182: powers of elements of A0 . An efficient solution to this problem was given in [1].

185: 3     First Algorithm
186: In this section, we describe the high-level structure of our algorithm. For this
187: section only, we assume that K is algebraically closed, that arithmetic in K
188: is unit-cost, and that we are provided with an efficient algorithm for factoring
189: univariate polynomials over K. These strong assumptions are to simplify the
190: high-level description. Once the algorithm is understood, we will describe in the
191: next section how to remove these assumptions.
192:      Most of the techniques used here, such as the Newton polygon, are well known
193: [2, 7, 15]. However, as mentioned in the introduction, one novel feature of our al-
194: gorithm is that we do not extend to the field of Puiseux series to obtain local
195: parameters, but reparametrize directly to obtain local parameters in the func-
196: tion field itself. This approach allows us to give an explicit description of the
197: coefficients occurring in the computation and analyze their bit complexity that
198: will be useful in the analysis of the next section.

202: 3.1   Overview
203: 
204: We are given an irreducible polynomial f (x, y) ∈ K[x, y]. The algorithm builds a
205: rooted labeled tree. Each vertex τ in the tree is labeled with a reparametrization
206: fτ (xτ , yτ ) of f (x, y), along with some other information ∆τ that specifies a set
207: of places Pτ of R. The tree grows at the leaves as more information becomes
208: available that allows us to split or refine the set Pτ . The information is calculated
209: from the Newton polygon of fτ (xτ , yτ ).
210:      The edges of the tree are labeled with positive integers giving ramification
211: information, along with coefficients of birational transformations. If τ is a child
212: of σ, then the integer labeling the edge (σ, τ ) gives the ramification index of xσ
213: over xτ , and the birational transformation gives xτ and yτ in terms of xσ and
214: yσ .
215:      The information ∆τ is a Boolean combination of constraints of the form
216: h(xτ , yτ ) ∈ P or h(xτ , yτ ) ∈ I, where the symbols P, I range over places of R
217: and their unique maximal ideals, respectively. The set Pτ is the set of places of
218: R satisfying these constraints.
219:      We first do a precomputation involving discriminants to find all exceptional
220: places of K(x), and reparametrize so as to move these places to the origin. (Even
221: this step will be difficult without the assumptions above). We now want to resolve
222: the point (0, 0). In other words, we have fτ (xτ , yτ ) and ∆τ = {xτ ∈ I, yτ ∈ I},
223: thus we want to find all places of R whose maximal ideal contains xτ and yτ ,
224: along with their local parameters and ramification indices over K(x).
225:      We cause the tree to branch at a vertex τ by adding new constraints that may
226: partition the set of places associated with that vertex or give more ramification
227: information. The new constraints are obtained from the Newton polygon of fτ .
228: We continue to expand the tree at the leaves, reparametrizing, adding more
229: constraints, and refining the partition, until each leaf τ determines a unique
230: place of R and xτ is a local parameter.
231:      When we are done, the ramification index of the unique place of R associated
232: with a leaf τ is given by the product of the integers labeling the edges along
233: the path from the root to τ . The composition of the birational transformations
234: labeling the edges along the path gives xτ and yτ in terms of x and y.

366: 4     Second Algorithm
367: Suppose that the coefficients of f lie in a subfield k of K. The algorithm of
368: the previous section is polynomial time, assuming unit-cost arithmetic in finite
369: extensions of k and the ability to factor. If we count the cost of the representation,
370: a naive approach may require exponential time.
371:    In this section we describe an implicit representation of the algebraic numbers
372: used in the algorithm of the previous section that allow them to be manipulated
373: using only arithmetic in the field k. We will use gcd heavily, but factorization is
374: unnecessary. This technique is called passive factorization and has been used by
375: Dicrescenzo and Duval [5, 6] and Teitelbaum [13]. We use this in conjunction with
376: the squarefree decomposition algorithm of [1] to avoid intermediate coefficient
377: swell when k = Q.
378: 
379: 4.1   Overview
380: Each of steps 3, 4, and 8 of the algorithm of Section 3 factored a polynomial
381: q(y), producing roots a. For each such a, we created a new child τ of the current
382: vertex σ and associated a with τ . The reparametrization of fσ to obtain fτ
383: involved the algebraic number a.
384:     Here, instead of factoring q to obtain the algebraic numbers a, we will just do
385: a squarefree decomposition of q using the algorithm of [1] to give finitely many
386: pairwise relatively prime factors qτ of q. We will create one new child τ for each
387: such factor qτ and associate qτ with τ . Subsequently, all computation involving
388: roots a of qτ will be done symbolically by introducing a new indeterminate a
389: and working modulo qτ (a). In effect, we will be dealing with all the roots of qτ
390: simultaneously in one subtree, instead of having a separate subtree for each root
391: as in the previous section.
392:     It may happen that some later computation causes qτ (a) to split further. This
393: will occur when a discrepancy in the behavior of the resolution over two different
394: 
395:                                           8
396: roots of qτ (a) is discovered. This discovery takes the form of another polynomial
397: in a that has a nontrivial common factor with qτ (a). When that occurs, we can
398: return to τ and split qτ using the gcd algorithm, then split τ into a separate
399: vertex for every new factor of qτ (a), replicating the entire subtree below each
400: new vertex. The tree never gets too big because of the absolute bound n on the
401: number of places.
402:     It may happen that qτ never splits. In that case the resolution over all roots
403: of qτ looks exactly the same, and the number of the places determined by the
404: subtree below τ can just be multiplied by the degree of qτ . Thus we have a single
405: node representing multiple places, but we know how many and their ramifica-
406: tions.
407:     Formally, at any vertex in the tree at any point in time, we have sequences
408:            a = a0 , a1 , a2 , . . . , ak                                                          (3)
409:             q = q0 (a0 ), q1 (a0 , a1 ), q2 (a0 , a1 , a2 ), . . . , qk (a0 , a1 , . . . , ak )   (4)
410: of indeterminates and polynomials describing them. The polynomials q gener-
411: ate a zero-dimensional variety V (q) in K k+1 . Arithmetic on coefficients will
412: be done modulo these qi . We maintain the invariants that each qi is reduced
413: modulo q1 , . . . , qi−1 and that the qi are squarefree. We also maintain the invari-
414: ant that the coefficients of qi , considered as polynomials in the indeterminates
415: a1 , . . . , ai−1 , are relatively prime to qi−1 .
416:      These conditions are determined by signs (zero or nonzero) of various sub-
417: resultants, which are minors of the Sylvester matrix [8]. These are polynomials
418: p(a0 , a1 , . . . , ai−1 ) in the coefficients of qi . For each such p, either its sign is de-
419: termined uniquely by q, i.e. p either vanishes on all of V (q) or does not vanish on
420: all of V (q), which allows the computation to be carried on; or p and qi−1 have a
421: nontrivial common factor, i.e. p vanishes on some nonempty subset of V (q) and
422: does not vanish on some other nonempty subset, in which case qi−1 splits and
423: we get a refinement. When all the splitting is done, we again have the property
424: that p(a) either vanishes on every point of V (q) or on no point of V (q).
425:      The key idea being exploited here is the same used in the BKR algorithm
426: for the theory of real closed fields [1], namely that we do not need to know the
427: algebraic numbers a themselves to solve the resolution problem, but only the
428: signs of certain polynomials in these algebraic numbers. This idea leads to an
429: efficient implementation of the passive factorization method of [5, 6, 13].

488: 5   Analysis
489: 
490: The tree is of small depth, since at each vertex, either there are multiple children;
491: or m > 1, in which case we get ramification (the maximum is n, and they are
492: multiplicative along edges); or the degree of the discriminant strictly decreases
493: [2, Theorem 15.1]. The number of branches is bounded by n, since there are at
494: most n places in all.
495:     There are at most as many qi at any vertex as the depth of the vertex. The
496: splitting of the tower (4) may cascade, but each such split uses only subresultant
497: computations and takes polynomial time. There are at most n splits since each
498: one creates a new branch of the tree. The product of the degrees of the qi is
499: at most n, since each sequence of roots (3) represented by the qi determines a
500: distinct place.

17:                                               Abstract. Let C be a plane curve given by an equation f (x, y) = 0
18:                                               with f ∈ K[x][y] a monic squarefree polynomial. We study the prob-
19:                                               lem of computing an integral basis of the algebraic function field K(C)
20:                                               and give new complexity bounds for three known algorithms dealing
21:                                               with this problem. For each algorithm, we study its subroutines and,
22:                                               when it is possible, we modify or replace them so as to take advantage

36:                                         1    Introduction
37:                                         When handling algebraic function fields, it is often helpful –if not necessary– to
38:                                         know an integral basis. Computing such bases has a wide range of applications
39:                                         from symbolic integration to algorithmic number theory and applied algebraic
40:                                         geometry. It is the function field analogue of a well-known and difficult problem:
41:                                         computing rings of integers in number fields and, as often, the function field
42:                                         version is easier: the algorithm of Zassenhaus [25] described for number fields in
43:                                         the late 60’s can indeed be turned into a polynomial-time algorithm for function
44:                                         fields which was later precisely described by Trager [23].
45:                                             However, there are very few complexity results going further than just stating
46:                                         a polynomial runtime. Consequently, most of the existing algorithms in the lit-
47:                                         erature are compared based on their runtimes on a few examples and this yields
48:                                         no consensus on which algorithm to use given an instance of the problem. In this
49:                                         paper, we provide complexity bounds for three of the best-known algorithms to
50:                                         compute integral bases and provide complexity bounds based on state-of-the art
51:                                         results for the primitives they rely on.
52: 2       Simon Abelard
53: 
54:     In this paper, we focus on the case of plane curves C given by equations
55: of the form f (x, y) = 0 with f ∈ K[x][y] monic in y and squarefree. We set
56: the notation n = degy f and dx = degx f . The associated function field is
57: K(C) = Frac (K(x)[y]/f (x, y)), it is an algebraic extension of degree n of K(x).
58: An element h(x, y) of K(C) is integral (over K[x]) if there exists a monic bivari-
59: ate polynomial P (x, y) such that P (x, h(x, y)) equals 0 in K(C). The set of such
60: elements forms a free K[x]-module of rank n and a basis of this module is called
61: an integral basis of K(C).
62:     Computing integral bases of algebraic function fields has applications in sym-
63: bolic integration [23] but more generally an integral basis can be useful to handle
64: function fields. For instance, the algorithm of van Hoeij and Novocin [13] uses
65: such a basis to “reduce” the equation of function fields and thus makes them
66: easier to handle. The algorithm of Hess [11] to compute Riemann-Roch spaces
67: is based on the assumption that integral closures have been precomputed. This
68: assumption is sufficient to establish a polynomial runtime, but a more precise
69: complexity estimate for Hess’ approach requires to assess the cost of computing
70: integral closures as well.
71: 
72: Our contribution. We provide complexity estimates for three algorithms ded-
73: icated to computing integral bases of algebraic function fields in characteris-
74: tic 0 or greater than n. To the best of our knowledge, no previous bounds
75: were given for these algorithms. Another approach which has received a lot
76: of attention is the use of Montes’ algorithm. We do not tackle this approach
77: in the present paper, a complexity estimate has been given by Bauch in [2,
78: Lemma 3.10] in the case of number fields. Using the Montes algorithm, a lo-
79: cal integral basis of a Dedeking domain  A at a prime ideal p is computed in
80: O n1+ε δ log q + n1+ε δ 2+ε + n2+ε δ 1+ε p-small operations, with δ the p-valuation
81: of Disc(f ) and the cardinal of A/p.
82:     Our contribution is actually not limited to a complexity analysis: the algo-
83: rithms that we present have been slightly modified so that we could establish
84: better complexity results. We also discuss possible improvements to van Hoeij’s
85: algorithm in some particular cases that are not uncommon in the literature. Our
86: main complexity results are Theorems 1, 2 and 3. Note that we count field oper-
87: ations and do not take into account the coefficient growth in case of infinite fields
88: nor the field extensions incurred by the use of Puiseux series. We also made the
89: choice not to delve into probabilistic aspects: all the algorithms presented here
90: are “at worst” Las Vegas due to the use of Poteaux and Weimann’s algorithm,
91: see for instance [21, Remark 3].
92:     We decided to give worst-case bounds and to only involve n and Disc(f ) in
93: our theorems so as to give ready-to-use results. Our proofs, however, are meant
94: to allow the interested reader to derive sharper bounds involving more precise
95: parameters such as the regularity and ramification indices of Puiseux series.
